correctness.rationale: Aliabadi's cycle-tiling theorem and subgroup-support theorem were checked in the primary full text. In \(H\), a simple product-one word over \(\{s,t\}\) is either \((s,s)\), \((t,t)\), or a cyclically alternating word. Simplicity makes a repeated adjacent involution close a 2-cycle, while an alternating word has length \(2a\), product \((st)^a\) or \((ts)^a\), and hence needs \(n\mid a\); simplicity bounds the length by \(2n\), leaving only the Hamiltonian length \(2n\). If all tiles have size two, they are edges of the alternating Cayley cycle \(C_{2n}\); its only two perfect matchings are the two color classes, giving \(q=0\) or \(2n\). The Hamiltonian alternating word gives \(q=n\). The subgroup-support theorem then decomposes an ambient realization into \(m\) such blocks, so the reachable counts are exactly the multiples of \(n\). The inspected exhaustive checker independently reproduces \(q\in\{0,n,2n\}\) for \(3\le n\le10\); this finite check is corroborative only.
correctness.risk: The theorem classifies only two-involution-supported multisets, not all quotient-realizable multisets of a dihedral group.

value.rationale: The theorem resolves a natural all-order dihedral slice of a recently introduced realizability problem, converts two isolated small-group patterns into a structural divisibility law, and propagates it to arbitrary ambient finite groups through subgroup support. This is a motivated classification lemma rather than an arbitrary finite census.
value.risk: It remains a two-letter slice and does not settle the full dihedral classification problem.

final_claim: Let \(G\) be finite and let \(s,t\) be distinct involutions with \(n=\operatorname{ord}(st)\ge3\). If \(H=\langle s,t\rangle\) and \(m=[G:H]\), then the full-size multiset with \(q\) copies of \(s\) and \(2nm-q\) copies of \(t\) is quotient-realizable in \(G\) exactly when \(n\mid q\); in \(H\cong D_{2n}\) the only possibilities are \(q=0,n,2n\).
limitations: Finite enumeration through \(n=10\) is supplementary only; the universal statement rests on the symbolic cycle/matching proof.
